newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai bourse sets movement limits for shares.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai bourse sets movement limits for shares.

text.p: The Shanghai Stock Enchange on Friday set a daily movement limit for all shares and funds at 10 percent in either direction with effect from next Monday, an exchange announcement said.
The announcement said that from Monday, daily price movments of all domestic A shares, foreign exchange B shares and investment fund units must not exceed 10 percent in either direction.

"Within any one trading day, the upward or downward movements of prices of the above-mentioned items, with the exception of those making their debut, must not exceed 10 percent against the closing price of the previous trading day," it said.
"From Monday on, all bids and asks exceeding the limits are null and void," it said. "No brokerage must accept invalid bids and asks."
The announcement said the trading limits had been approved by the China Securities Regulatory Commission, which supervises all Chinese securities and futures markets.
Securities officials in Shenzhen, informed of the move, expressed surprise and said they knew of no such plan on the Shenzhen stock exchange.
Shanghai brokers said the announcement followed weeks of dramatic price movements both up and down despite repeated warnings against over-speculation from the central authorities.
Shanghai's B share index surged more than 80 percent in the three weeks up to Tuesday on expectations that Beijing would take measures to boost the market.
It has since fallen more than 20 percent on fears that the securities authorities might take measures to restrict domestic Chinese trading B shares.
Shanghai's A share index has surged more than 100 percent in a bull run since April with prices of some shares soaring more than 300 percent.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission has in recent months issued a series of rules concerning risk control and punished many brokerages for irregularities with the aim of cooling the markets down.
Brokers said they believed the price limits are likely to greatly cool down investment zeal in Shanghai with liquidity expected to flow southward to the Shenzhen market.
